division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.7(1)  A contingency fee agreement must
(a) be in writing, and
(b) be signed by the lawyer and the lawyer’s client or by their
authorized agents.
(2)  To be enforceable, a contingency fee agreement must contain
the following particulars in precise and understandable terms:
(a) the name and address of each client;
(b) the name and address of the lawyer;
(c) a statement of the nature of the claim;
(d) a statement of the event or contingency on which the
lawyer’s fees are to be paid to the lawyer;
(e) a statement about
(i) the manner in which the contingency fee is to be
calculated, provided that no fee, calculated as a
percentage or otherwise, may be payable on
disbursements or other charges recovered,
(ii) the maximum fee payable, or the maximum rate
calculated, detailing the disbursements and other
charges that are included in that fee or rate or
indicating that disbursements and other charges are
in addition to that fee or rate, and
(iii) whether the client is responsible to pay
disbursements and other charges, and if so, a general
description of the types of disbursements and other
charges likely to be incurred, other than relatively
minor disbursements;
(f) if the lawyer is to receive any amount from a costs award,
a statement that
(i) the cost award is intended to be a complete or partial
reimbursement of the lawyer’s charges to the client,
(ii) the cost award is owned by the client and that by
signing the contingency fee agreement the client is
waiving the right to any amount from the costs award
that is payable to the lawyer in accordance with
subclause (iv),
(iii) the amount from the costs award retained by the
lawyer will be in addition to the lawyer’s percentage,
fixed fees or other form of legal fees, and
(iv) the percentage of the costs award that the lawyer may
receive may not exceed the percentage of the
judgment or settlement that the lawyer is entitled to;
(g) a statement that, if the client gives notice in writing to the
lawyer within 5 days after the client’s copy of the
contingency fee agreement is served on the client, the
client may terminate the contingency fee agreement
without incurring any liability for the lawyer’s fees, but
that the client is liable to reimburse the lawyer for
reasonable disbursements;
(h) a statement that
(i) at the request of the client, a review officer may
review either or both of the contingency fee
agreement and any lawyer’s charges in an account
rendered under the agreement, and
(ii) either or both of the contingency fee agreement or
any lawyer’s charges may be further reviewed by
way of an appeal from a review officer’s decision to
a judge.
(3)  The contingency fee agreement must be witnessed by a person
who sees the client sign the agreement, and that person must then
swear an affidavit of execution.
(4)  The client must be served with a copy of the signed
contingency fee agreement within 10 days after the date on which
the agreement is signed, and an affidavit of service to that effect
must be executed by the person who served the agreement.
(5)  A client may terminate a contingency fee agreement without
incurring any liability for the lawyer’s fees under the agreement if
the client, within 5 days after service on the client of the copy of
the contingency fee agreement, gives written notice of the
termination to the lawyer, but the client is liable to reimburse the
lawyer for reasonable disbursements incurred by the lawyer.
(6)  If a contingency fee agreement provides that a lawyer is
entitled to an amount from a costs award, the lawyer is not entitled
to receive from the costs award any higher percentage of the
judgment or settlement than the lawyer is entitled to receive under
the contingency fee agreement.
(7)  Every account rendered under a contingency fee agreement
must contain a statement that at the client’s request a review officer
may determine both the reasonableness of the account and the
reasonableness of the contingency fee agreement.
(8)  An account that does not contain the statement required by
subrule (7) is of no effect unless the Court
(a) is satisfied
(i) that the omission of the statement was inadvertent,
and
(ii) the client has not been misled or prejudiced,
and
(b) the Court waives the requirement for the statement.

BOOK_A.commentary:
A. Cross References
See also R.10.8 and commentary on it.
B. History
At common law, quite possibly an agreement could not make the lawyer’s payment depend on
results of litigation, but for years Alberta Rules have allowed such an agreement if the formalities
prescribed (referred to above) are observed.¹
C. Scope
The previous Rules contained a real deﬁnition of a contingency fee agreement, but the
deﬁnition in the 2010 Rules is superﬁcial and circular, evidently directed only to cross-reference
other Rules. This Rule has always been regarded as conﬁned to litigation retainers, given the
history of the Rule and the background of the common law or champerty. But one decision²
extends the Rule to a retainer on sale of land. Another decision reduced it on the ground that the
claim settlement with the government achieved was political, not lawyers' work!³
D. Form and Breaches
An agreement over legal fees need not be in writing unless it makes payment contingent on
results.⁴
If it is so contingent, it binds the client only if the formalities in R.10.7 are observed.⁵
Proof of timely service on the client is vital under R.10.7(4).⁶
And the notice on the bill of costs
about the right to review under R.10.7(7) is also important.⁷

Minor non-compliance with R.10.7 is no bar to applying the contract.¹
The court can weigh the
effects of breaches, and forgive ones doing little or no harm.²
Even several technical breaches of
the Rules about conditional-fee agreements need not upset the agreement if the purpose of the
requirements in the Rules were met.³
In one case, lack of an afﬁdavit of service would have done
no harm.⁴
But in another case, giving no maximum fee, no description of how costs awards were
to be shared, and no afﬁdavit of execution, were too serious to overlook, so the agreement was
invalid.⁵
Or where it omitted the required provisions for excluding disbursements from fees (and
said the reverse), who owns party-party costs, if the fee is a complete payment of fees (partly),
how to terminate the agreement, and right to have the court review the fee (in the agreement or
the bill).⁶
A clause allowing the law ﬁrm in its discretion to move fees up or down depending on later
events, made it impossible for the client to know the maximum fee possibly chargeable, which
R.10.7(2) (e) requires, even if the client is fairly sophisticated, so the court would not forgive that
omission.⁷
If the agreement is silent about who keeps costs which the opponent is ordered to pay
this client, R.10.7(2) does not apply because it speaks only of cases where the lawyer is to receive
any amount from a costs award, so there could not here be any breach of that subrule.⁸
Rule
10.7(2) (h) (ii) calls for a statement of the right of appeal to a judge, and a mandatory arbitration
clause violates that, as it would probably bar an appeal; certainly the right to appeal was not
stated “in precise and understandable terms”.⁹
The subparas. of R.10.7(2) (g) about service and
right to cancel within a few days after service, and an afﬁdavit of execution, are important and the
three are interlinked. No service, no witness, no afﬁdavit of service, and not reciting the precise
terms of when the deal may be cancelled, were fatal.¹⁰
They were especially important as this client
and law ﬁrm had dealt with each other for years, but always on an hourly-rate basis, and the client
had to understand clearly how different was this conditional-fee agreement.¹¹
Subrules 10.7 (7), (8) require certain contents of an account from a law ﬁrm to its client, where
a conditional-fee agreement governs the fee. Not all were in this account, and a mere recital in
the account that it was pursuant to the Fee Agreement did not sufﬁce. There must be a speciﬁc
statement, not a mere reference back to the Fee Agreement. This was too important to forgive.¹²

If the agreement is unenforceable, the court should be slow to award a fee about equal to
the amount which the agreement would have yielded, especially if minor children are among the
clients or beneﬁciaries.¹
E. Review
The court sets out a number of rules for a review ofﬁcer reviewing a contingency contract and
bill.²
The cases are reviewed in the Rusk decision.³
Even if the lawyer is the applicant before the review ofﬁcer or the court, the lawyer does not
have the onus of proving internal workings or procedures of the client organization to approve the
agreement, especially if there is no evidence that they were not followed, because only the client
knows that.⁴
Many proposed criticisms of a contingency agreement which have no legal force, because the
law does not impose any such duties, are reviewed.⁵
First the review ofﬁcer (or a judge) should interpret a retainer or a contingency fee agreement,
using ordinary principles of contractual interpretation.⁶
Only after that, should the ofﬁcer or judge
get to the question (if it arises) of whether a contingency fee agreement is unreasonable and so
should be varied.⁷
A retainer agreement is judged objectively, and as of the day it was signed, looking at the
interests and expectations of both parties. That includes their ﬁnancial circumstances, knowledge,
likely attitude of the opponent, likely duration of the tasks, risks and who pays disbursements.⁸
The size of the sum recovered is not the only test of quality of outcome; often counsel's
efﬁciency, and comparison with likely recovery, are more important.⁹
There is no rule of thumb
that a 20% contingency agreement cannot be too high; amount of recovery and work done are
also relevant.¹⁰
The review ofﬁcer should not assume that lawyers are unused to extensive negotiation, or that
smaller or rural law ﬁrms are, especially if neither side alleges that.¹¹
It overstates to say that the review ofﬁcer “owes deference” to the agreement?¹²

If a costs award makes any use of the winner’s expenses (e. g. x percent of them), that
incorporates into the award any contract about fees between the winner and his or her lawyer,
and the party paying costs has an interest in the fee agreement and a right to full disclosure of it.¹
F. End of Retainer
The lawyer's ceasing to act for good reason (e. g. client’s refusing to take advice) does not
affect reasonableness of fee or contingency agreement.²
G. What is Fairness
It is not helpful to speak of “heavy burdens” on the lawyer.³
The review ofﬁcer need not give effect to a contingency fee contract if it is found to be unfair.
The unfairness may come from how the contract was negotiated, or from the fact that when made
it set too high a rate of payment. That means either unfair at the time that it was made, looking only
at facts which were then known or should have been known, without hindsight; or unfair because
of later unexpected events.⁴
If the agreement was fair, it binds the review ofﬁcer.⁵
Though a contingency fee contract usually involves an imbalance of power and information,
the court should not set one aside without good cause; such contracts are valuable, and certainty
is necessary for both parties.⁶
It may be relevant that a complex, expensive suit may make a contingency agreement the only
way for a client who is not wealthy to bring this suit.⁷
Some criteria for evaluating fairness and reviewing a contingent fee are set out.⁸
Thirty to 40%
fee (depending on how far the suit progresses) is fair for high-risk suits like medical malpractice,
but not for ordinary motor-vehicle cases, especially if party-party costs are also to go to the
lawyer.⁹
Thirty-ﬁve percent was too high for a tobogganing accident settled early for $3 million.

25% is within the range usually negotiated in Alberta for contingency agreements.¹
The court gave
what it assessed at double the usual large hourly rate, but under half what the fee contracted for
would have been.²
Twenty-ﬁve percent was too high where a claim was already accepted and
the work was almost clear cut, and the risk minimal; $250 per hour was substituted.³
A judge
(reviewing the review ofﬁcer) cut the contracted 20% down to 5%, taking judicial notice that that is
what real estate agents charge to sell buildings.⁴
Such an agreement can provide for an escalating
percentage if the suit becomes longer and more contested.⁵
H. Miscellaneous
The client does not owe any implied duty of good faith to the lawyer, nor of settling the suit only
in a way which will protect the lawyer’s best interests.⁶
How to calculate a contingency fee where the recovery was not a lump sum, is an exercise in
mathematics and actuarial science, not arbitrary.⁷
Where the client is an infant, the court’s power to review comes from a number of sources.⁸
A client with experience of making land deals (a landman) has above-average capacity to
understand and negotiate legal agreements such as contingency fees.⁹
Only Alberta’s Class Actions Act requires advance approval of a contingency fee agreement.
It is proper to give notice to the Public Trustee if many or most of the people involved in the class
would not be sui juris. Notice ordinarily would not be given to the defendant.¹⁰
There is a lengthy
discussion of the criteria.¹¹
The law restricting champerty still exists, and so a solicitor cannot take an assignment of his
or her client’s cause of action, before judgment, even if the client has become insolvent well into
the lawsuit, nor can the solicitor ﬁnance the client’s lawsuit.¹²

BOOK_B.title: Contingency fee agreement requirements

commentary.text: Rule 10.7 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.7. 1. Overview In Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation v. Rath and Company Barristers and Solicitors, 2024 ABKB 258, Justice Simard set out the Court’s approach to Rule 10.7: [16] The aim of contingency fees is to make court proceedings available to people who could not otherwise afford to have their legal rights determined. This goal should be encouraged and a flexible approach should be taken to problems arising from contingency fee arrangements, in order to facilitate access to the courts for more Canadians: MS v DM, 2014 ABQB 702 at para 37. It is also the case, however, that the people who rely on contingency fee agreements “are often vulnerable due to poverty, impact of injuries, educational status or other social disadvantages” and the Rules of Court and other rules governing contingency fee agreements offer some protection to this potentially vulnerable group: MS at para 38. Therefore, when a court is interpreting a contingency fee agreement or considering its fairness, “the necessity and importance of encouraging this form of legal fee arrangement should be balanced with the need to safeguard the citizens who rely on contingency fee agreements in order to have access to justice.”: MS at para 39. The Court’s Approach to Rule 10.7 Cases [17] While a flexible and balanced approach is called for when interpreting contingency fee agreements and deciding whether they are fair or reasonable, it does not apply with the same force, or to the same effect, in cases considering the mandatory requirements in the Rules of Court: MS at para 52. The language in Rule 10.7 and 10.8 is very clear and is mandatory: certain things “must” be in contingency fee agreements and contingency fee accounts, and certain procedures “must” be followed. If those things are not present or those procedures are not followed, the Rules state clearly that the contingency fee agreement is not enforceable. [18] Among the reasons for following a less flexible approach in these cases is that “Rule 10.7 is a consumer protection provision; it sets out requirements to ensure that the terms of the contingency fee are clear and to ensure that the client has executed and been provided with a copy of the agreement”: Barry v Industrial Alliance and Financial Services, 2022 ABKB 706 at para 13. Also, the requirements of Rule 10.7 “are not onerous and are easily incorporated into contingency agreements”: Stanchfield v Doe, 2023 ABKB 273 at para 21. [19] While the Court’s approach in Rule 10.7 cases is “less” flexible, that does not mean there is no flexibility whatsoever. This Court has drawn a line between “minor” or “technical” non-compliance with the Rules, from which it can grant relief, and more “serious” or “substantive” non-compliance with the Rules, which will be fatal to an agreement. The Court has articulated this distinction in slightly different ways: (a) “I agree that Rule 618 [the predecessor Rule to Rule 10.7] purposefully prohibits enforcement when there is non-compliance, but I find that the Rule should not be interpreted so inflexibly that the most minuscule and immaterial omission would prevent the enforcement of the agreement. Therefore, even though I confirm that defects in a contingency agreement will be strictly construed against the lawyer, the court is not without its judicial discretion to alleviate against minor technical oversights that are without import”: per Germain J in Sonnenberg v Schumacher & Associates, 2005 ABQB 352 at para 38; (b) “the flexible approach is more appropriate when considering more minor or technical departures from the rules”: MS at para 52; and (c) “In cases where the non-compliance is not minor or technical but undermines the client protection and clarity the rules are designed to create, courts must be careful not to reward counsel, or prejudice clients, for counsel’s non-compliance.”: Stanchfield at para 21. [20] As noted recently by Graesser J in Mikisew Cree First Nation v Rath, 2023 ABKB 321 at para 86, “there is no bright line between minor and substantial irregularities”. Each case will turn on its specific facts. 2. The formal procedure mandated by Rules 10.7(2)(g), (3), and (4) In Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation v. Rath and Company Barristers and Solicitors, 2024 ABKB 258, Justice Simard set out the procedure required by Rules 10.7(2)(g) and Rules 10.7(3) and (4): [69] When they are read together, subrules 10.7(2)(g), (3) and (4) mandate a cohesive formal procedure for what is to happen when a contingency fee agreement is executed, and immediately afterwards: (a) a person other than the client must be present when the client signs the agreement, and that person must then complete an affidavit of execution. This adds heightened solemnity and formality to the signing of such agreements, providing an outward reminder to both parties of the extraordinary nature of contingency fee agreements, and the important consequences of signing them. The swearing of the affidavit of execution also ensures that there can be no dispute about the date on which the agreement was signed, which triggers service, the next step in the process; (b) the lawyer must then serve the agreement on the client within 10 days after the agreement is executed. In my view, the Court must place importance on the Legislature’s choice of the word “served” in Rule 10.7(4). The Rule does not say that the lawyer is to “deliver”, “give” or “send to” the client a fully-executed copy of the agreement. The lawyer must serve the agreement on the client, then complete an affidavit of service. Those words clearly connote formal service. I will address the issue of what particular type of service is required, below; (c) the lawyer formally serving their client with a fully-executed copy of a contingency agreement will again impress on the client the heightened solemnity and importance of what it has agreed to and, even more importantly, it may draw to the client’s attention its right to terminate the agreement without penalty, within five days after being “served”, i.e. the exact statement in the agreement that is mandated by Rule 10.7(2)(g) (I note that the client’s substantive right to terminate is provided in Rule 10.7(5). Rule 10.7(2)(g) does not create the termination right; rather it requires the lawyer to insert notice of that termination right in the agreement). Obviously, if the mandated statement is not present in the agreement, formal service by the lawyer is less likely to fulfil this purpose; (d) the lawyer must then complete an affidavit of service, which performs the important function of ensuring that there can be no dispute about when the client was served, starting the five-day optional termination period, and when the termination right expired; and (e) the client has five days after being served with the executed agreement, to give written notice of termination to the lawyer. If the client terminates in this period, the client will not incur any liability for the contingency fee but will be liable only for reasonable disbursements. If the client does not terminate in this five-day period, it will be obligated to pay the contingency fee. … [73] Subrules 10.7(2)(g) and 10.7(4) use the terms “served” and “service” but they do not specify what type of service is required. Our Court of Appeal addressed the concept of service in Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corporation, 2012 ABCA 266, a dispute about whether claim disallowances in a bankruptcy had been properly served. The Court commented at paras 18 – 19: The legal concept of service was discussed in Zahmol Properties Ltd. v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at paras. 14-6, 522 AR 32: Service is a specialized form of notice. While “notice” is sometimes used as a synonym for “knowledge”, in this context notice encompasses the conveying of knowledge or information with intention to affect legal rights. For example, the exercise of an option in a contract conveys the information that the contractual right is being exercised, and that the legal rights of the optionor and the optionee will be affected. A casual statement of an intention to exercise the option at a future time may convey “knowledge”, but not in a way that fixes legal rights. The concept is illustrated by the decision in St. Peter’s Evangelical Lutheran Church v. Ottawa, 1982 CanLII 60 (SCC), [1982] 2 SCR 616. By statute a municipality could prevent the demolition of a historic building, provided that notice that the municipality did not consent to the demolition was given within 90 days. The council of the municipality adopted a resolution within the 90 days, denying permission to demolish the building. The owners of the building were aware of the resolution, because two of its representatives were present when the resolution was passed, and it was reported in the newspapers, but no formal notice of the resolution was ever given. While conceding that no formal notice had been given, the municipality argued that the actual knowledge of the resolution was “notice in fact”. The Supreme Court of a ruled at p. 629 that it was an error to equate “knowledge on the part of the appellants with notice given by the respondent City”. The Court held that some type of “notice” to fix the legal rights of the parties was needed in addition to mere knowledge of the resolution. Service of legal process conveys the information that an action or proceeding has been commenced that may affect the rights of the person being served, with an intention to affect or engage legal rights. The party served is put on notice that it must take steps to protect its rights, or the court or tribunal might adjudicate in its absence. Sometimes legal processes are commenced in order to crystallize rights, without a final decision having been made as to whether the action will be triggered by service and prosecuted. Sometimes knowledge of an action or proceeding is conveyed without intending to affect legal rights, as when a “courtesy copy” of legal process is provided. Where the knowledge of the legal process is conveyed without an intention to affect legal rights, there is generally no “service”: Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223 at paras. 103-7, 34 Alta LR (4th) 199; Bennett v. Cultural Tours (1991), 58 BCLR (2d) 225. In order to demonstrate proper service of the disallowances of the claims, it must be shown that the respondents received notice of the disallowances of their claims, in a context that made it clear that their rights were being engaged. [74] Thus, it is apparent that service is a somewhat flexible concept. However, the core requirement is that the party being served receives effective notice that their legal rights may be affected. As I noted above, one of the important purposes of the service required by Rule 10.4 is that the client is effectively notified or reminded of their right to terminate a contingency fee agreement within the cooling off period. Because the notice mandated in Rule 10.7(2)(g) must state that the termination period commences when the client is “served”, it follows logically that when a client receives a fully-executed contingency agreement from their lawyer under Rule 10.4, the client must be made to understand that it has been “served”. Only if it knows that it has been served will it know that its five-day termination period has started running. Therefore, at a minimum, to comply with Rule 10.4, a lawyer’s correspondence to their client must expressly use the term “served” or “service”.
